extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, editorial board members, and researchers interested in publication ethics and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative standards for how journal editors (including EiCs, associate editors, and editorial board members) should identify, disclose, manage, and be held accountable for conflicts of interest in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must carry COI statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should carry a COI statement that reflects their past history, as well as actual relationships and positions that they have, as these may influence their editorial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements should describe relationships and positions (past and present) that could influence editorial decisions; disclosure should be visible to readers and the research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of conflict of interest (WAME-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A COI exists when 'there is a divergence between an individual’s private interests (competing interests) and his or her responsibilities to scientific and publishing activities such that a reasonable observer might wonder if the individual’s behavior or judgment was motivated by considerations of his or her competing interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard to assess whether an editor's private interests could be perceived to influence editorial behavior; applies to editors, authors, reviewers, journals, institutions, funders, media, and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad PLoS definition of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing interest is anything that interferes with, or could reasonably be perceived as interfering with, the full and objective presentation, peer review, editorial decision-making, or publication of research or non-research articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing interests can be financial, non-financial, professional, or personal and may relate to institutions, organizations, or persons; adopt broad definitions like PLoS to capture non-financial COIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and disclose non-financial COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-financial COIs (personal, political, academic, ideological, religious, status-seeking, unpaid memberships, prior co-authorship, shared institutional affiliation) should be identified and disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although harder to define, non-financial COIs can be powerful influences; journals should consider requiring disclosure of these, not only financial ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure as a COI management method
rubrics_metrics.description: One method is full disclosure, where authors, reviewers, and editors acknowledge having non-financial interests which might influence their reporting or review, or where there is a possibility that the publication will affect their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should ask for explicit written statements (or confirm absence) from editors, reviewers and authors at submission or appointment; however, disclosure alone may not be sufficient—combine with other management steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal / delegation when conflicted
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors who believe that a conflict will preclude impartial judgment should disclose the nature of the conflict and decline to handle the paper; manuscripts should be delegated to other editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journal policies explicitly require recusal; delegation to co-editors or outside editors reduces bias. COPE/CSE recommend delegation/recusal in cases of departmental, collaborator, competitor relationships, or specific interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assigning manuscripts to clearly conflicted editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal submissions are assigned to editors in an effort to minimize potential conflicts. Relationships considered conflicts and avoided include current colleagues, recent colleagues, recent co-authors, and doctoral students for which editor served as committee chair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no editor is conflict-free, assign the least-conflicted co-editor and ensure independent peer review; require editors to report conflicts after assignment as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish editors' names, affiliations and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must provide the full names and affiliations of the journal’s editors on the journal’s website as well as contact information for the editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about editorial membership and how to contact editors supports accountability; follow COPE guidance to list this information publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare COIs to publisher/employer and update them
rubrics_metrics.description: Any potential editorial conflicts of interest should be declared to the publisher in writing prior to appointment, and then updated if and when new conflicts arise; the publisher may publish such declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers often require written disclosure on appointment and periodic updates; failure to disclose can be disciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must not handle submissions with close personal/professional ties
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor must not be involved in decisions about papers which s/he has written him/herself or have been written by family members or colleagues or which relate to products or services in which the editor has an interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such submissions must be subject to the journal's usual procedures with peer review handled independently of the relevant editor/research group, and there must be a clear statement on any published paper indicating independent handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers must declare and act on conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should inform the editor of any potential competing interest and decline to review when such a conflict exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should avoid reviewing manuscripts with recent collaborations, shared employment history, or other interests; inform editors during review if potential conflicts arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must disclose all relevant conflicts and funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should disclose in their manuscript any financial or other substantive conflict of interest that might be construed to influence the results or their interpretation, and disclose all sources of financial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponding author is responsible for providing declarations for all co-authors; journals may require specific forms or statements at submission and a statement in the published article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized published statements about competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The published article should include a standard sentence indicating whether the authors declare competing interests or not (e.g., 'The authors declare competing financial interests: details accompany the full-text' or 'The authors declare no competing financial interests').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For double-blind review, provide minimal statements during review and full disclosures at acceptance; do not require monetary values but require the nature of interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential handling of declarations during review (varies by journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals treat authors' declarations as confidential until publication; others disclose them to peer reviewers during review depending on peer review model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a clear policy on whether reviewer and editor see full declarations during review; for double-blind systems provide minimal statements to preserve anonymity while signalling presence/absence of COIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit use of unpublished materials from submissions for personal research
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished materials disclosed in a submitted manuscript must not be used in an Editor’s own research without the explicit written consent of the author(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers must keep privileged information confidential and not use it for personal advantage; include explicit prohibitions in COI policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual disclosure and record-keeping (IEEE example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals in editorial or decision-making roles shall submit a completed Conflict of Interest Disclosure Statement (e.g., annually or within 30 days of assuming position) and forms shall be on file; failure to submit may result in removal from service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/societies should set timelines for initial and periodic disclosures and enforce consequences for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and exemplify types of conflicts to declare
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of conflicts include financial (stock ownership, patents, paid employment, consultancy, honoraria, grants, gifts), personal (relationships or disputes with authors, collaborators), and professional (membership of advisory councils, public associations with industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide non-exhaustive lists to guide editors/authors/reviewers what to declare; require authors/editors to list potential interests or explicitly state none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate review to outside/independent editors when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an editor has a COI, many journals (e.g., Croatian Medical Journal) hand over the review process to an outside editor so the risk of bias can be prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent editors or external handling editors to avoid perceived or actual bias; document the delegation process in journal records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid author-suggested reviewers to limit bias and fake peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Move away from author-suggested peer reviewers, which may be biased, fake or carry COIs, to an editorial system in which editors are exclusively responsible for conducting peer review themselves or for finding and recruiting suitably qualified peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce reliance on author-provided reviewer lists; implement safeguards against fake reviewers and editorial gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply transparency standards to editors as to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publishers should expect of themselves what they expect of others — apply the same standards of transparency (about COIs, recruitment, qualifications) that journals expect of authors/reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish editorial recruitment and approval processes and academic qualifications of editors; make COI policies public and enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure correction of the record and active post-publication review
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the correction of the literature when errors are detected during post-publication peer review; journals should commit to PPPR and to correcting mistakes discovered after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have processes for responding to PPPR complaints, investigating image manipulation or data issues, and issuing corrections/retractions as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish formal arbitration or oversight for COI disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the existence of a scientific arbitration board or other formal body that looks at the lack of disclosures between editors and authors or between advertisers and editors to ensure selection is not reflecting hidden commercial or other COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create independent oversight mechanisms (internal or external) to adjudicate COI complaints and enforce policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce accountability including removal for editorial failure
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be due process where editors have failed, including their removal from an editorial board; editorial failure includes abuse of position, failure to correct literature, or managing COIs improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define failure modes, investigation procedures, and sanctions (including removal) in publisher/journal governance documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent coercive citation and metric gaming by editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must not abuse their position to enhance their own work or profiles or to game the metrics system by suggesting excessive citation of their work or of their journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor citation practices for coercion; include policies prohibiting requests for unnecessary self- or journal-citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require COI statements from all participant roles (E, A, R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and journals commonly require declarations from editors (E), authors (A), and reviewers (R) — 'All conflicts of interest should be declared by the author, editor or reviewer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COI policies should cover all parties involved in publishing; specify where and how declarations are recorded and published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow COPE flowcharts and best-practice guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a conflict of interest is suspected, journals should follow established flowcharts (e.g., COPE) to manage suspected conflicts and to investigate and resolve issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt COPE guidance for investigations, corrections, retractions, and conflict resolution processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explicit declaration even if no COI exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should request a statement from authors/editors/reviewers to confirm whether conflicts exist; if none, the individual should confirm in writing that no conflicts exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit 'no conflict' statements in submissions and published articles to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality of certain declarations when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals may treat authors' declarations as confidential until publication; alternative arrangements should be specified (e.g., double-blind review minimal statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance transparency and confidentiality requirements; clearly communicate to contributors how their declarations will be used and when they will be disclosed.
